_meta.directives: Fiche recentrée sur le nom (2026-10-03), passe de correction : chaque piste d'origine est attribuée à qui la porte et citée à la page dans les notes de sa source ; aucune n'est retenue comme la bonne. Ne pas étendre sans source dédiée.

oralTraditions.claim: The Konaté, the Coulibaly and the Keïta are said to descend from the three children of Mahamadu Kanu and Mariatu, each the founder of a clan. The narrative circulates in two versions. In the first, the eldest, Coulibaly, yields power to the younger, Keïta, in exchange for food. In the second, three brothers live in the same village; during a famine, the third, Lauali Simbo, shares the game equally and the villagers choose him as chief. As he has no child, his brother Kanunyoro takes the name Konaté, "the one who has children"; then children are born to Lauali, who receives the name Keyita, from ke, "the inheritance", and ta, "to take". The dictionary of Mandinka clan names, for its part, records a common origin with the Kulibali.
oralTraditions.collector: V. Vydrine et A. Davydov, dont les matériaux sont publiés par E. A. Bogacheva
oralTraditions.context: Narrative reported in Russian in a university thesis of 2017, with no indication of place or informant

oralTraditions.claim: The epic announces the story of the "son of the Buffalo" and the "son of the Lion"; an editor's note specifies that the lion is the totemic ancestor of the Keïta, so that Soundiata is the son of the Lion through his father and the son of the Buffalo through his mother. The dictionary of clan names also lists jàra, the Bambara word for the lion, among the clan's prohibitions.
oralTraditions.carrier: Djeli Mamadou Kouyaté, griot de Djeliba Koro, près de Siguiri
oralTraditions.collector: Djibril Tamsir Niane, qui l'a traduit en français
oralTraditions.context: Epic published in 1960 and its notes

oralTraditions.claim: The griot relates that at the very beginning the Manding was a province of the Bambara kings, and that those now called Maninka are not autochthonous: they come from the East. Bilali Bounama, ancestor of the Keïta, is said to have been the faithful servant of the Prophet, and his eldest son Lawalo is said to have left the Holy City to settle in the Manding. There follow Latal Kalabi, Damal Kalabi, then Lahilatoul Kalabi, the first Black prince to make the pilgrimage to Mecca, and his grandson Mamadi Kani, the hunter king.
oralTraditions.carrier: Djeli Mamadou Kouyaté, griot de Djeliba Koro, près de Siguiri
oralTraditions.collector: Djibril Tamsir Niane, qui l'a traduit en français

oralTraditions.claim: The Keïta trace their origin to Bilal ibn Rabah, the first muezzin of the Muslim community. The griot schools of the Manding count sixteen kings before Soundiata, with lists that differ from one school to another; those of Siguiri give Lahilatul Kalabi as the first pilgrim king. The historian who gathers these traditions notes that the adoption of Muslim ancestors from the East was common in the royal courts of the region, and that the ancestor claimed here is a Black man from Abyssinia, not a white ancestor; he himself places Mamadi Kani around the early twelfth century and Maghan Kön Fatta, father of Soundiata, in the early thirteenth century.
oralTraditions.collector: Djibril Tamsir Niane, d'après les écoles de tradition orale du Manding
oralTraditions.context: Historical synthesis published by UNESCO in 1985

oralTraditions.claim: One tradition brings the founders of Mali from the east, from Kong, led by Kabala Simbo Keïta, ancestor of Soundiata; they are said to have settled in the country of Do. In this version, Kita is not the cradle of the Keïta: Soundiata is said to have subdued it by defeating the Kamara, before making it his second capital after Kangaba. The thesis that reports it notes that the version of an origin at Kong may have arisen at Kong, as that of an origin at Kangaba at Kangaba, well after the events, and that the main shrines of the Keïta today lie well south of Kita.
oralTraditions.collector: Charles Monteil, auteur de l'époque coloniale, d'après des informateurs qu'il ne nomme pas
oralTraditions.context: Text dated 1924, cited at second hand in a university thesis of 2017

linguisticReconstructions.claim: No dictionary consulted gives an established meaning for the word: the dictionary of Mandinka clan names writes it Kéyità, with the forms Kétà and Kɛ́yità, and defines it only as a clan name.

One explanation links the name to that of the town of Kita. It is put forward without convincing evidence, and a tradition reported above makes Kita instead a conquest of Soundiata, not the cradle of the Keïta.

One explanation, reported in 1912 by a colonial administrator on the basis of local traditions he does not name, links the name to the nickname of a king of Mali, Allakoï: he answered "Alla koï", "God, indeed", to any question about the cause of an event, and some add that his descendants were called "those of Allakoï", a name later shortened to Koïta or Keïta. No other source consulted repeats it, and it does not agree with the narrative that derives Keyita from ke, "the inheritance", and ta, "to take".

The cradle of the clan is said to be the country of the Manden mountains, around the towns of Dakadiala, Naréna and Kiri, where the Keita were anciently settled. This is a historian's synthesis; the tradition reported above has them come from farther away.
The dictionary of jamuw links the entry Kéyità to the regions of Kita, the Manding and Farana, without saying whether these are places of origin or of settlement.

sources.title: EthniAfrica — fiche du peuple Malinké, organisation clanique
sources.notes: Taken from the "Clan organisation" chapter of the fiche of the Malinké people.

sources.title: Soundjata ou l'épopée mandingue
sources.notes: Niane, Djibril Tamsir, Présence Africaine, 1960. Transcription of the narrative of the griot Djeli Mamadou Kouyaté of Djeliba Koro (Siguiri); it is a written record of an oral tradition. Pages read on the digitised archive copy at archive.org (SoundjataOuLepopeeMandingue), close to the printed edition without being identical to it: the story of the son of the Buffalo and the son of the Lion (p. 10); the note making the lion the totemic ancestor of the Kéita (p. 11, note 3); Bilali Bounama, ancestor of the Kéita, Lawalo and the line of the Kalabi (p. 12); Mamadi Kani, the hunter king (p. 13).

sources.title: Bamadaba — dictionnaire des noms claniques (jamuw)
sources.notes: Appendix of clan names of the Bamadaba, the electronic Bambara-French dictionary of the Corpus bambara de référence (Bailleul, Davydov, Erman, Maslinsky, Méric, Vydrin, 2011-2020, CC BY-NC-SA), pointed out by Vydrin in Mandenkan 63, 2020, p. 89-110. Complete file consulted. The entry Kéyità gives the forms Kétà and Kɛ́yità, Malinké, Dia and Bobo groups, equivalents (including Souma, Koné and Beawɔgi), the regions of Kita, the Manding and Farana, jàra (the lion) among the prohibitions, as joking partners Turɛ, Kulibali, Sisɛ, Sidibɛ, Kaba, Wulare, Jane and Màriko, and a note, written in Russian and translated here, on a common origin with Kulibali; it carries no status and gives no meaning for the name. Joking relations are not always reciprocal from one entry to another: each pair is cited from the entry that carries it.

sources.title: Pouvoir, places et filiation : les senankuya au Mali
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, Cahiers de praxématique, number 38, 2002, p. 175-197. Field survey in Mali. It states what the pact requires: the relation holds in perpetuity for all the descendants of the two lineages, marriage between them is prohibited — applied in varying ways today, it specifies — and mutual aid is owed without reservation. Cited for the obligation itself; it does not name the pair of this fiche, which the entries cited alongside it carry.

sources.title: Pactes, alliances et plaisanteries. Pratiques locales, discours global
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, and Smith, Étienne, Cahiers d'études africaines, number 184, 2006, p. 687 ff. Cited for the caution it carries: the idea that joking kinship soothes conflict is treated there as a hypothesis inherited from Radcliffe-Brown and taken up by conflict-resolution studies, hence as a discourse to be analysed and not as a measured effect. The first page is verified, the last page is not.

sources.title: Manden Charter, proclaimed in Kurukan Fuga, Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, UNESCO
sources.notes: Inscription of 2009. The notice describes a charter proclaimed in the early thirteenth century by the founder of the Mali empire and an assembly of sages, whose words are transmitted orally from father to son within the Malinké clans. It does not mention sanankuya.

sources.title: Charte de Kurukan Fuga : mémoire et communauté, Amadou Saïbou Adamou, Magana, 2023
sources.notes: Cites article 7 of the charter: "there is instituted among the Mandenkas the Sanankunya (joking cousinage) and the Tanamanyöya (a form of totemism)". Places the oral assembly around 1236 and specifies that the text was restored by griots during a seminar at Kankan, in Guinea, in 1998, then translated into French and published in 2008.

sources.title: The World Won't Listen: The Mande Hunters' Oath and Human Rights in Translation, Gregory Mann, Humanity, 2022
sources.notes: Notes that the celebration of these charters has aroused scepticism among those who question their origin, hence their age, and refers to the work of Jan Jansen, who reads them as interventions in a contested cultural politics.

sources.title: Histoire générale de l'Afrique, IV : L'Afrique du XIIe au XVIe siècle — chapitre 6, Le Mali et la deuxième expansion manden
sources.notes: UNESCO, ed. D. T. Niane, 1985; chapter by D. T. Niane. Printed pages: the Keita tracing their origin to Bilal ibn Rabah, Lawalo founder of Kiri, the cradle of the Keita around Dakadiala, Narena and Kiri (p. 153, note 28), and the adoption of Muslim ancestors from the East, a common practice in the courts of the region, Bilal being a Black man from Abyssinia (p. 153, note 31); the line from Lawalo to Mamadi Kani, placed around the early twelfth century, Maghan Kön Fatta in the early thirteenth, and the sixteen kings before Soundiata whose lists vary from one griot school to another (p. 154); Nare Fa Maghan, father of Soundiata (p. 158). The chapter gives no meaning for the name.

sources.title: Histoire générale de l'Afrique, V : L'Afrique du XVIe au XVIIIe siècle — chapitre 12, Du Niger à la Volta
sources.notes: UNESCO, ed. B. A. Ogot, 1999; chapter by M. Izard and J. Ki-Zerbo. Printed page: joking kinship between Koulibali (Kurubari) and Keita or Touré, given as an indication of very ancient relations between Bambara and Malinké (p. 372).

sources.title: Les noms de clan du Manden (jamu) dans les sources africaines, occidentales et arabes
sources.notes: Bogacheva, E. A., bachelor's thesis, Saint Petersburg State University, 2017, in Russian; supervised by A. Davydov, reviewed by V. Vydrin. Entry Kéyità, p. 82-84: the lion among the clan's prohibitions (p. 82); the narrative of the three brothers, given with no indication of place or informant among the materials gathered by V. Vydrine and A. Davydov, and the link with the name of Kita, put forward without evidence (p. 83); the explanation through "Alla koï", cited from Maurice Delafosse, Haut-Sénégal-Niger, 1912, volume II, p. 175 (p. 83-84); the tradition of an origin at Kong reported by Charles Monteil, with the thesis's caution about local versions (p. 84). A bachelor's thesis is not a peer-reviewed publication: it is cited for the testimonies it transmits.

gaps.reason: We have found no source that attributes a hereditary status or function to the name. The dictionary of Mandinka clan names carries no status for the entry Kéyità, although it gives one for other names; this silence does not establish the absence of a status, it says only that no source consulted indicates one.

No namesake lineage of distinct origin has been found. The jamu is borne well beyond the dynastic descent, by affiliation and by adoption, but this is an extension of the same name and not a second origin. The dictionary of jamuw likewise brings Kéyità, Kétà and Kɛ́yità together under a single entry and lists Souma, Koné and Beawɔgi among its equivalents.
